**The Lampwright**

*Type:* Ambient/wandering monster — a hunched, cloak-like figure made of soft grey wax, with a hollow socket where its face should be and a burning wick sprouting from the top of its head.

**Backstory:**

When the underground was first sealed, the monsters trapped inside had no sun, and the caverns were pitch dark. A guild of craftsmen took it upon themselves to light the way — carving lanterns, tending the great pit-fires, memorizing every tunnel so that no one would be lost. They called themselves Lampwrights.

But light in the underground has a price. The old texts say a flame down here cannot burn on oil alone; it must be fed on *memory*. So every lamp the guild lit cost them something — the name of a friend, the shape of their mother's face, the reason they'd started in the first place. They gave willingly, tunnel by tunnel, until the caverns glowed and the Lampwrights themselves had nothing left to remember. Their bodies softened into wax. Their faces guttered out.

Now they wander the passages they built, still trying to help travelers, still holding up their little flames — but they can no longer recall the way anywhere. A Lampwright will walk ahead of you for hours with total confidence, lighting your path down corridors it has never seen, growing shorter and dimmer as it goes.

**Gameplay hook:** Lampwrights are harmless and can illuminate dark areas, but they burn down as they follow you. A player can extend a Lampwright's life by *telling it a story* — giving it a memory to burn. Naturally, the memories on offer are the child's own, and each one spent is a small piece of the surface world the player forgets: a parent's voice, the taste of rain, the color of their own front door. Late in the game, the player may find they no longer remember what they were climbing toward.

**The Lampwright (species: Glimmerwick)**

**Appearance:** A hunched, wax-skinned creature about the height of a ten-year-old, with a hollow chimney of a head from which a single candle-flame burns. Its "face" is whatever expression it has scratched into its own wax that morning — so its mood is always a day out of date. Its hands are permanently blackened from trimming wicks.

**Backstory:** When the monsters were driven underground, the deepest caverns had no light at all, and the first generations went blind within a decade. The Glimmerwicks were not born — they were *made*, molded from candle wax and grave-tallow by monster artisans desperate to give their children something that could see for them. Each Lampwright was bound by a single instruction: *carry the light ahead of the ones who follow.*

Centuries later, the underground has lanterns, phosphor moss, and glowstone. Nobody needs a Lampwright. But they still walk the old tunnels in slow processions, lighting corridors no one uses, replacing candles in shrines to monsters long dead. They cannot stop; the instruction is the only thing holding their wax together. Their great private terror is not being extinguished — it's being *followed by no one.*

**Encounter idea:** A Lampwright will attack a human child on sight, not from hatred, but because a child walking behind it means it has a purpose again — and it will do anything to keep you from walking *past* it. Spare it by letting it lead you somewhere, even the wrong way. It will light the whole path, weeping wax, absurdly grateful.

**The Lanternjaw**

**Appearance:** A hunched, dog-sized creature with a body like knotted driftwood and a mouth that hangs permanently open, wedged wide by its own overgrown lower teeth. Inside that mouth floats a small, cold flame — pale green, flickering, never touching the flesh around it. Its eyes are milky and useless.

**Backstory:** Lanternjaws weren't born underground. They were the pets and pack-animals of the first monsters driven below, back when the tunnels were unmapped black and no one knew which passages ended in air and which ended in stone. The monsters fed them a rare mineral that burns cold, and the creatures learned to hold the flame in their mouths and walk ahead of the caravans, sniffing out the routes with breathable air.

Generations of that work bred the sight right out of them. They navigate by smell and by the draft on their teeth. And they never stopped working — long after the monsters settled and built cities and forgot the old migrations, the Lanternjaws kept walking the deep tunnels in slow loops, lighting paths for caravans that no longer come.

**In play:** A Lanternjaw that notices a lost child will assume its old duty has resumed. It won't fight — it will simply turn and start walking, pausing whenever you fall behind, and it will lead you unerringly toward *fresh air.* Which is not always the same thing as *out.* Sometimes it's a ventilation shaft too narrow for a body. Sometimes it's a crevasse. The Lanternjaw has no concept of a destination — only of moving air — and it will wait patiently at the edge of a thousand-foot drop, flame guttering, for you to follow.

Players who understand this can use them deliberately: a Lanternjaw is a living compass for airflow, invaluable for mapping the flooded lower caverns. Players who trust them blindly tend to end up somewhere with a very nice breeze.

**The Lanternjaw**

A hunched, slow-moving monster the size of a large dog, with a body like cracked slate and a hinged lower jaw that hangs open permanently. Inside that jaw hangs a small flame — pale blue, flickering, never consuming. Lanternjaws have no eyes.

**Backstory:**

When the underground was first sealed, the monsters who fled deepest found themselves in tunnels where no light had ever reached. Some of them gave up their eyes to the dark — a bargain made with the caverns themselves, or simply the slow work of generations. What they got in return was fire: a cold ember kindled in the throat, fed by memory rather than fuel.

A Lanternjaw's flame burns brighter the more it remembers. Elders glow like torches; hatchlings barely spark. And because they cannot see, they navigate by the warmth their light throws back off the walls — which means a Lanternjaw that forgets too much goes blind in every sense, and simply stops.

So they became keepers. Not of treasure, but of stories. Travelers who share news, gossip, or grief with a Lanternjaw will find its flame swell and the tunnel ahead suddenly bright. Travelers who lie to one will find the fire gutter — Lanternjaws can taste a false memory, and they find the flavor unbearable.

They gather in the old rest-stops along the deep roads, hundreds of them murmuring in a language of clicks and pops, endlessly retelling each other everything they've been told. Much of the underground's true history survives only in their jaws, garbled and lovingly mispronounced.

**Game hook:** Lanternjaws function as lore-dispensers and light sources, but the player must "feed" them by sharing something true — potentially a mechanic where the child recounts a real memory of the surface, and the game tracks which memories they've spent.

**The Lampwrights (Lumenkin)**

A species of soft, moth-like monsters with translucent bodies and a hollow cavity in their chests where a small flame is meant to burn. They stand about waist-high to an adult, walk upright on four spindly legs, and speak in a papery whisper that gets louder the brighter their flame.

**Backstory:**

Before the underground was sealed, the Lampwrights were the world's lanterns. They had no fire of their own — instead, they were *given* light. A surface-dweller would kindle a Lampwright's chest with a candle, a hearth-coal, a wish spoken aloud, and in exchange the creature would guide that person safely through the dark for as long as the flame lasted. It was a fair trade, and the Lampwrights were proud of it. Their whole culture was built around *being* useful to someone.

Then the world above closed its door, and no one came to light them.

Generations later, the Lampwrights are nearly all dark. They've built an enormous, beautiful, unlit city in the deepest caverns, and they maintain it obsessively — polishing lanterns nobody lights, sweeping roads nobody walks. Some have gone slightly mad from purposelessness, wandering the tunnels asking strangers, over and over, *"Do you need me? Are you lost? Are you sure you're not lost?"* A few desperate ones have tried to steal flame from other monsters, which is deeply taboo — a stolen light burns green and eventually eats the thief hollow.

**Why they're useful in your game:** The child protagonist is *exactly* the thing the Lampwrights have been waiting for — a surface-dweller who is genuinely, definitionally lost. A player who lights a Lampwright gains a companion and a light source, but the flame is finite, and the Lampwright will follow them all the way to the surface door and then have to decide whether to step through into a world that no longer needs lanterns. Alternatively, a player could exploit them — take the guidance, never light them, leave them dark — which is a nicely quiet kind of cruelty for a game about mercy.

**Design notes:** Their dialogue could visibly dim as their flame runs low (text fading, font shrinking). And an unlit Lampwright's chest cavity makes an obvious inventory slot — the player might be tempted to store *items* in there, which they'd find humiliating and would absolutely comment on.

**The Hollowbell**

A Hollowbell looks like a stooped figure in a heavy woolen cloak, hood empty except for a small brass hand-bell suspended where a head should be. When it moves, the bell doesn't ring — it *un*-rings, swallowing nearby sound and leaving a pocket of dead silence a few feet wide.

**Backstory:** Long before the underground world was sealed off, its cities kept criers — monsters whose whole purpose was to carry news between the deep districts. They were bred for perfect memory and beautiful voices, and each was given a bell at birth that they were forbidden to ever put down.

When the surface war ended and the monsters were driven below, the last order given to the criers was to announce the sealing of the great door. They rang their bells and shouted the news through every tunnel and hollow for eleven days, until their voices tore out entirely. The grief of the message did the rest: the criers hollowed themselves, unwilling to ever carry news again.

Now they wander the old routes out of habit, absorbing sound because they cannot bear to make any. They are not hostile — in fact, they're gentle, and old monsters still tip their hats to them out of respect. But a Hollowbell will follow anyone who speaks kindly to it, and its silence is contagious: linger too long in its company and you may find your own voice going quiet, then thin, then gone.

**Game hook:** Hollowbells are useful — their silence can mute alarms, sleeping beasts, or a collapsing corridor. But every use costs the player a line of dialogue permanently. Talk too much with a Hollowbell as your companion, and by the time you reach the surface, you'll have no way left to tell anyone where you've been.

## The Hollowmourn (or "Lamplighters")

**Appearance:** Tall, gaunt figures of soft grey wax, roughly humanoid but slumped and drippy, as though they've been left too close to a fire. Where a face should be there's only a smooth depression with a single wick sprouting from the center, burning with a small cold blue flame. The taller and older a Hollowmourn is, the shorter its wick — some elders are barely more than guttering stubs, hunched and half-melted into the cave floor.

**Backstory:** When the underground world was sealed off, the monsters left behind had no sun, no stars, and no way to measure the passing of time. The first Hollowmourn were volunteers — ordinary monsters who agreed to be "rendered," transformed into living candles so their neighbors would have light. It was meant to be an honor and a temporary sacrifice.

Nobody told them the flame would burn their memories as fuel.

Generations later, the Hollowmourn are the underground's undertakers, archivists, and lamp-posts — silent figures standing at crossroads and doorways, faithfully illuminating a world they can no longer remember caring about. They speak in fragments of other people's recollections, things they've absorbed from those who sat by their light and talked. A Hollowmourn might greet the player with a stranger's wedding vows, or a soldier's last words, without knowing what any of it means.

They are not hostile. They are worse than hostile: they are *helpful*, and they will follow a warm, memory-rich human child anywhere, drawn to the smell of a life still being lived. Standing too near one for too long makes you forget things — a friend's name, why you were angry, the color of the sky.

**Gameplay hook:** A Hollowmourn companion can light the deepest tunnels where nothing else will burn, but every area you cross with it costs you something — a journal entry blanks out, an NPC you'd befriended no longer recognizes you, a puzzle solution you'd written down goes missing. The mercy option is to give one your memory of the surface, willingly, which snuffs its flame and lets it finally rest.

## The Lampwrights

**Appearance:** Tall, thin figures of fused wax and soot-blackened brass, roughly humanoid but stooped, with a hollow lantern where a head should be. Inside each lantern burns a small flame — no two the same color. Their "faces" are simply whatever the flame casts on the frosted glass: a flicker of a smile, a wavering frown. Their wax hands are permanently melted into the shapes of the tools they used in life.

**Backstory:** Long before the monsters were sealed underground, the Lampwrights were the ones who maintained the great lightways — mile-long chains of oil lamps that let the deep cities pretend at daylight. When the seal came down and the surface was lost, the underground's supply of lamp oil went with it. The lightways went dark within a generation.

The Lampwrights refused to let the dark win. They developed a ritual to render their own bodies into fuel: a slow, voluntary transmutation into wax and flame. Each one now burns with the last of their own life, tending the few lamps that remain and stretching that fuel as thin as it will go.

The catch, and the tragedy, is that a Lampwright's memories burn off along with the wax. The oldest among them are barely more than a foot tall, guttering, and can no longer remember *why* they must keep the lamps lit — only that they must. The younger ones care for their elders devotedly, refilling them with scraps of tallow and candle-ends, knowing exactly what they're looking at.

**Game hooks:**
- They fear the player's presence — a child from the surface means the seal is weakening, and if it breaks, the lightways could be relit. Some Lampwrights desperately want this. Others have burned so long that being made *unnecessary* is the only thing left to be afraid of.
- One tiny, nearly-spent Lampwright follows the player around, and the running quest is figuring out what it's forgotten it was trying to tell you.
- Their flames are all different colors because the color reflects who they were. A Lampwright can tell you a stranger's whole personality by glancing at their light — but has no idea what color its own flame is.

prompt: Write a short story that has three main characters Alice Bob and Mallory.
generations:
**The Handshake**

Alice ran the bookshop on Vesper Street, and every Thursday at four she left a paperback on the third shelf from the bottom, spine facing inward. Bob came at five, browsed for exactly nine minutes, and left with it under his arm. Neither of them had ever spoken to the other.

That was the arrangement. It had worked for two years.

The message was never in the book — that would be careless. It was in *which* book. *Moby-Dick* meant the shipment was delayed. *Jane Eyre* meant proceed. *The Count of Monte Cristo* meant someone was watching.

On the third Thursday of October, Alice shelved *Jane Eyre*.

At five o'clock, the bell above the door rang, and a woman came in. Grey coat, wet umbrella, an apologetic smile. She went straight to the third shelf from the bottom, ran her finger along the spines, and pulled out *Jane Eyre*.

"How much?" she asked.

Alice's hands went still on the register. "That one's spoken for."

"Is it?" The woman turned the book over, thumbing the pages as though checking for underlining. "It's just sitting on a shelf. Anyone could take it."

"Someone's coming for it at five."

"It's five now."

Alice looked at the clock. It was 4:58. She looked at the door. Through the rain-streaked glass she could see a figure across the street, hesitating at the curb — Bob, in his brown jacket, waiting for the light.

"Four pounds," Alice said.

The woman paid in coins, exact change, and left. The bell rang. Bob crossed the street, came in at 5:01, went to the third shelf from the bottom, and found nothing there at all.

He stood for a long moment. Then he picked up the book beside the gap — *The Count of Monte Cristo* — brought it to the counter, and paid without a word.

Alice put the coins in the drawer. Her hands were steady now. She had known, the moment the woman's finger touched the spine, that the system had a flaw they'd never named: it assumed only two people knew the language. It had never occurred to either of them that someone might simply *learn* it, standing in the rain outside a bookshop on Vesper Street, week after week, watching which books came and went.

Bob left. Alice locked the door at six, turned the sign, and went to the back room where she kept the ledger no one else had ever seen.

She wrote: *Thursday. Jane Eyre taken by third party. Grey coat. Exact change — she'd counted it out beforehand. She's been planning this.*

Then she wrote, underneath: *Which means she doesn't know I keep a ledger. Advantage: mine.*

Somewhere across the city, Mallory sat on a bench with a paperback she couldn't read a word of the real message in, and began, patiently, to build a bookshop of her own.

**The Man in the Middle**

Mrs. Petrakis seated her seventh-graders alphabetically by first name, which is how Alice Nguyen came to sit in the desk by the window, Bob Ferraro by the pencil sharpener, and Mallory Weiss precisely, fatefully, between them.

It began in September with a folded square of paper.

*Do you have the notes from Friday? I was out sick.* — A

Mallory received it with her left hand and passed it with her right, the way you'd pass a plate at dinner. That first month she didn't read them. She wasn't that kind of person yet.

But in October Alice started drawing little cartoons in the margins — a stick figure of Mrs. Petrakis with lightning bolts for hair — and Mallory couldn't help but see, and once she'd seen she couldn't help but look, and once she'd looked she found she was hungry for it in a way she couldn't explain to herself.

The notes were about nothing. That was the astonishing part. *My brother put a whole hot dog in the toaster.* *I think the janitor is a retired assassin.* *If you had to fight one horse-sized duck or a hundred duck-sized horses.* Nothing at all, and Mallory read every word twice before folding them back along their creases.

In November she changed one.

Bob had written: *Want to work on the volcano project at my house Saturday?*

Mallory sat with it for the length of a lecture on the causes of the First World War. Then she took out her pen — she had practiced Bob's handwriting in the back of her math notebook, the way he made his *y*'s like fishhooks — and she added a line.

*Also Mallory should come. She's good at that stuff.*

Alice wrote back: *ok! ✓*

And that Saturday there were three of them in the Ferraro garage with baking soda and a coffee can, and Bob was confused for about four minutes and then wasn't, because he was thirteen and easily distracted by explosions. The volcano erupted orange across the concrete. Mallory laughed so hard she had to sit down on an overturned bucket, and Alice sat down next to her, and something in Mallory's chest went loose and warm and terrifying.

She should have stopped there. She knew it even then.

But December came, and with it a note from Alice that said *Bob do you think Mallory is annoying, be honest*, and Mallory's hands went cold, and she did not pass it. She wrote a new one instead: *Bob do you want to come to my birthday thing on the 14th.*

Bob wrote: *yeah!!*

There was no birthday thing. Mallory's birthday was in April. She had to invent a stomach flu and then a cancellation and then, when Bob asked about it in January, a whole cousin.

That was how it went. She was in the middle and the middle was a country with its own weather. She learned that Bob thought Alice was smarter than him and minded, a little. She learned that Alice's father had moved to Sacramento and that Alice had told exactly one person, and the person was Bob, and Mallory read it in the girls' bathroom with the note pressed flat against her knee and cried, and then folded it up and passed it on, unaltered, because there are things you don't touch.

It ended in March.

Alice and Bob had gotten clever. Somewhere in February they'd started writing in a cipher — a dumb one, a letter-shift, but the shift changed every day according to a rule Mallory couldn't crack, because the rule had been agreed on out loud, somewhere Mallory wasn't. In the cafeteria, maybe. On the bus.

For two weeks she carried gibberish back and forth like a waiter with a covered dish.

Then on a Tuesday, Bob's note came through and it wasn't in cipher at all. It said:

*Mallory. We know.*

She looked up. They were both watching her — Alice by the window with her chin on her fist, Bob half-turned in his chair, and neither of them looked angry, which was worse than anything.

She waited all day for the ax. It came at three-fifteen, by the bike racks, in the form of Alice Nguyen standing with her arms crossed and Bob a step behind her holding both their backpacks.

"Why," Alice said.

Mallory had rehearsed a hundred answers. What came out was: "You never wrote to me."

Nobody said anything. A bus groaned out of the lot.

"You sat *right there*," Alice said finally. "You could have just — talked."

"I know."

"You made up a *cousin*."

"I know."

Bob shifted the backpacks. "The volcano thing was you?"

"Yes."

"Huh," he said. "That was a good day."

Alice turned on him. "Bob."

"It *was*."

And Alice opened her mouth to argue and then didn't, because it had been, and she was not a liar, whatever else she was.

They made her sit on the curb while they conferred by the fence, and Mallory watched a beetle cross the asphalt and thought about how she would have to survive lunch every day for the rest of her life. When they came back, Alice had a pen.

"New rule," she said. "You don't pass notes anymore. You *write* them. On the same paper. Your own line."

Mallory stared.

"Three lines," Bob said helpfully. "Like a stack."

"And if you ever forge anything again," Alice said, "I'll tell everyone about the birthday party that didn't exist."

"That's fair," Mallory said.

So that was the treaty. From March until June, one square of paper made the trip from window to pencil sharpener and back, and it carried three hands: Alice's tight left-slanted print, Bob's fishhook *y*'s, and Mallory's, cramped at first, then bolder, taking up space.

There was no security in it at all. Anyone could have read those notes. Mrs. Petrakis confiscated four of them and probably did.

But nothing in them was ever a lie again, and Mallory found — sitting in the middle, which she had never once left — that this was the only thing she had actually wanted, the whole time, and that she could have simply asked.

**The Middle**

Alice ran the bookshop on Coldwater Street, and Bob baked bread three doors down, and for eleven years they had been in love without either of them saying so.

They wrote letters. This was the absurd part, the part their friends would have mocked them for if their friends had known. Two people who could see each other's storefronts, who passed on the sidewalk most mornings, who could have simply *spoken*—and instead they wrote. Alice would write at closing, in the yellow lamplight among the unsold poetry, and drop the envelope in the blue box at the corner. Bob would write at four in the morning while the ovens came up to heat, flour in the creases of his knuckles, and mail his in the afternoon before he slept.

It had started as a joke. A postcard she'd sent him from a conference in Duluth, and his reply, and then it simply never stopped. Over eleven years, a language had grown between them, dense with private reference. They wrote things they could not have said out loud. It was easier to be brave with a stamp involved.

Mallory delivered the mail.

She had walked Coldwater Street for nine years, and she knew everything about everyone, which is the great unadvertised salary of the postal carrier. She knew who was behind on their car payments and who had a daughter at Northwestern and who received the catalogs they'd rather nobody saw. She knew Alice's handwriting the way you know a song's first three notes, and she knew Bob's, and she had known for years that the two envelopes crossing in her bag every day were the only interesting thing on her route.

For a long time she just liked knowing. It felt like being trusted, even though nobody had trusted her with anything.

She opened the first one in November, over a kettle in her kitchen, and told herself it was a single time, and read four pages about Alice's mother dying and how Alice had not cried at the funeral but had cried, hard, in the car outside a gas station in Kenosha eight days later, over nothing, over a song.

Mallory read it twice. Then she resealed it and delivered it, and Bob's reply came two days later, and she opened that one too.

It went on for eight months.

She learned that Bob had wanted to be an architect. She learned that Alice slept badly and had a recurring dream about a house with a room she could never find. She learned the shape of a thing being built, slowly, letter by letter, and she began to understand that they were closing in on something—that in one of these envelopes, soon, one of them was going to say it plainly, and then the letters would stop, because people who say it plainly don't need to write anymore.

They would get each other. And Mallory would get her route back: circulars, water bills, the beige nothing of other people's lives.

So she changed a word.

It was a small thing. Alice had written *I think we've waited long enough,* and Mallory, with a fine pen and steady hand, made it *I think we've waited too long.* Four letters. A hinge.

Bob read it at four in the morning and stood very still with the ovens ticking. He wrote back something careful and small, and Mallory read it and let it through, and Alice read *something careful and small* where she had expected the other thing, and the temperature of the correspondence dropped ten degrees.

After that it was easier. She trimmed a sentence here. She let a letter arrive four days late, so that an apology answered a question that had already curdled. She never wrote anything new—she wanted to be clear with herself about that—she only edited. She was not a liar. She was an editor.

By spring the letters had thinned to one a week, then one a fortnight, and they were about weather and inventory. Alice and Bob still passed on the sidewalk in the mornings and said hello with a kind of injured politeness, each believing the other had cooled, each too proud to ask.

Mallory told herself she had done nothing. Nothing had happened. That was, in fact, the whole point.

---

What undid her was ordinary: a paper jam of the human kind. In August, Alice's water heater burst, and she closed the shop for a day, and being restless she walked down to the bakery in the middle of the afternoon when she knew Bob would be asleep, just to sit on the bench outside it, and Bob—who had not slept, who had been lying awake for a year—came out to sweep the step.

They looked at each other.

"You stopped writing," she said.

"You stopped first."

"I did not stop first. I wrote you in November that we'd waited long enough and you sent me back a paragraph about *flour prices.*"

Bob set the broom against the wall. "You wrote that we'd waited too long."

There was a silence with a lot in it.

"I have it," he said. "I have all of them."

So did she. They spread eleven years across a bakery table that evening, four hundred and some letters, and read them in order, hers and his interleaved like a deck shuffled, and it took until two in the morning to find the seams: the pen that wasn't quite the pen, the paper that had been dampened and dried, the four-letter hinge.

Alice, who was not a shouter, said quietly, "Somebody has been standing in the middle of us."

---

Mallory came at eleven the next morning with the mail, as she had for nine years.

They were both waiting at the counter of the bookshop. On it, squared like evidence, were two letters.

She knew before anyone spoke. She had known, honestly, since November.

Bob said, "Why."

And Mallory found that she had no defense prepared, only the truth, which she had never once said out loud and which came out of her like something being pulled. "Because you were the only real thing on my route."

Nobody said anything.

"I have walked this street for nine years," she said. "I put the mail in the box and I keep walking. Nobody has ever written *me* a letter. Not once. Not in nine years." Her hands were shaking on the strap of her bag. "And I thought if I could just—stay near it a little longer—"

Alice's face did something complicated.

"You could have knocked," she said. "Any day. Any of nine years. You could have come in and said hello and I'd have made you coffee."

Mallory looked at the floor of the bookshop, at the worn place in front of the poetry, and understood that this was true, and that it was the worst thing anyone had ever said to her.

She resigned the route. She moved, eventually, one town over.

---

Alice and Bob married in the fall, quietly, and stopped writing letters, exactly as Mallory had predicted, because they no longer needed the postal service to be brave.

But on the first anniversary, and every year after, Alice wrote one anyway. She addressed it to a house one town over, and she never got a reply, and she sent it every year regardless, because she had learned something she could not put down: that the danger is never the message.

It's whoever's standing in the middle, holding it, wishing it were theirs.

**The Man in the Middle**

Alice lived in 4B and Bob lived in 4F, and between them ran a hallway with a carpet the color of old tea, and at the end of that hallway was a supply closet where Mallory kept the mops, the fuse box, and a folding chair he was not supposed to sit in during working hours.

It began with the radiators. In February the building's heat went feral — 4B boiling, 4F arctic — and Alice slid a note under Bob's door because the intercom had been broken since the Clinton administration.

*If you're cold, come sit in my apartment. It's ninety degrees in here and I'm growing orchids out of spite. — A, 4B*

Bob never got it. Mallory found it at six in the morning, half-swallowed by the tea-colored carpet, and picked it up the way he picked up everything: without thinking, out of habit, because his job was to make the hallway look like nobody lived there.

He read it in the supply closet with the door shut.

He should have slid it back under 4F. Instead he sat in the chair he wasn't supposed to sit in and thought about how long it had been since anyone had invited him anywhere, and then he thought — and this is the part he could never explain later — that the note was *funny*, and that Bob in 4F, who wore the same gray coat every day and said *morning* like it was a full sentence and a closed door, might not know it was funny.

So Mallory copied it out. He had good handwriting; his mother had been strict about it. And where Alice had written *out of spite* he wrote *out of spite, which is the only reliable fertilizer,* and he folded it and slid it under 4F.

Bob's reply came the next morning, tucked under 4B's door, where Mallory retrieved it at 6:04.

*I accept. I'll bring the only thing I own that's warm, which is a bottle of bourbon. Warning: I am bad company. — B, 4F*

Mallory read it four times. Then he wrote it out again, and where Bob had written *I am bad company* he wrote *I am out of practice at company, which is not the same as being bad at it.*

He told himself he was correcting a typo of the soul.

---

It went on for eleven weeks.

He got good at it. He learned Alice's slant and Bob's cramped capitals and could produce either in under a minute. He learned that Alice worked nights transcribing medical dictation and had a sister she didn't speak to, and that Bob had been a high school chemistry teacher until something happened that he only ever referred to as *the thing in April,* and that both of them, separately, had stopped answering their phones sometime in the last two years.

And he learned that when Alice was cruel about herself, Bob believed her, and when Bob was cruel about himself, Alice believed him, and that the only thing standing between these two people and a mutual agreement to be worthless was a fifty-six-year-old superintendent with a fountain pen and no business whatsoever in the matter.

So he stood there. He shaved the edges off. When Alice wrote *ignore that, I was drunk,* Mallory wrote *ignore that, I was honest, which is worse.* When Bob wrote *don't come Thursday,* Mallory wrote *come Thursday, but late.*

They came Thursday. He heard it from the closet: 4F's door, footsteps, 4B's door, and then nothing for four hours, and then laughing.

Mallory went home and slept better than he had in a year.

---

The thing about standing in the middle is that eventually the two ends move close enough to touch, and then there's no room for you.

In April — it was always April, apparently — Bob left a note that said *I want to tell you about the thing that happened. Not in writing. Come over at eight and I'll say it out loud.*

Mallory read it in the closet and felt the floor tilt. There was nothing to fix. It was the best sentence either of them had ever written. He slid it under 4B's door and went to change a fuse in the basement and stayed down there until nine-thirty.

At ten, Alice knocked on the closet door.

She was holding a shoebox. Mallory looked at it and knew, with the total calm of a man watching a wave from very close, exactly what was in it.

"He kept them," she said. "I kept mine. We laid them out on his floor tonight to read them in order." She opened the box. "The handwriting's mine. But I didn't write these."

Mallory stood up. It seemed like the least he could do.

"Say something," she said.

"I'm sorry."

"That's not — " Her voice cracked and she pressed the back of her wrist against her mouth. "Do you understand what you did? I spent eleven weeks falling in love with a man's *mind* and it wasn't his."

"It was his."

"You *edited* it."

"I didn't add anything that wasn't in there," Mallory said. "I took things out. He kept writing that he wasn't worth the trip across the hall. That's the only thing I ever deleted. Both of you. Over and over. Like it was a signature."

Alice stared at him.

"You want to know what I put in?" he said. "Nothing. I put in nothing. Eleven weeks, one hundred and forty-some notes, and every single word was yours or his. I just wouldn't let either of you say the worst thing about yourselves to the only person who was listening."

Behind her, Bob had come into the hallway in the gray coat, holding a piece of paper, and his face was doing something complicated.

"That's not your call to make," Bob said.

"No," Mallory agreed. "It wasn't."

Nobody said anything for a while. The building made its noises — pipes, someone's television, the elevator that had never once arrived when you wanted it.

"I've lived here nine years," Mallory said finally. "I know when everyone's mail comes. I know when everyone stops getting mail. I know which apartments smell like cooking on a Sunday and which ones don't." He looked at the mops. "4B and 4F were the two quietest doors on the floor. And then they weren't. And I did that, and it was the only useful thing I've done since my wife died, and I'd like to say I'm sorry and mean it, but I'm not sure I do."

Bob looked down at the paper in his hand. It was one of the early ones — Mallory could tell by the fold.

"*Which is not the same as being bad at it,*" Bob read aloud. He laughed, once, without much humor. "I've thought about that sentence maybe two hundred times. I built a whole year on it."

"It's true," Mallory said.

"You don't know that."

"I've been watching this hallway for nine years," Mallory said. "I know it."

---

They didn't get him fired. Alice wanted to for about six days and then didn't.

What happened instead was that in June, when the heat went feral in the other direction and 4B was arctic and 4F was boiling, a note appeared under the supply closet door, in two handwritings, one slanted and one cramped:

*Dinner Thursday. 4F, 8pm. Bring the chair — the one you're not supposed to sit in. We're told you're bad company. We'd like to check the source.*

Mallory read it in the closet, with the door shut, four times.

Then he brought the chair.

# The Channel

Alice lived on the third floor of Rosewood Manor, in the wing they called Cedar, and Bob lived on the first, in Birch. Between them lay two staircases, one elevator with a broken button panel, and, since March, a laminated sign on every fire door that read **NO RESIDENT MOVEMENT BETWEEN WINGS.**

They had met in the dining hall in February, which felt now like another geological era. Bob had asked whether she intended to eat her dinner roll. Alice had said no, and then had spent forty minutes explaining to him why the crossword in the *Herald* had gone soft since the new editor took over. Bob had listened the way a man listens when he has decided something.

Then the doors closed, and the only thing that moved between floors was laundry, medication, and Mallory.

---

Mallory was twenty-four and worked doubles, and had a laugh you could hear from the far end of a corridor. She had been the one to suggest it, actually — she found Alice crying into a paperback and said, "Write it down. I'll take it to him."

So Alice wrote it down.

*Bob — They've put me on the puréed diet, which is an insult I intend to survive. Are you keeping up with the crossword? Tuesday's had four errors. Four. — A.*

Mallory folded it into her scrub pocket and carried it down two flights, and that evening she came back up with Bob's reply, written in a hand that slanted hard to the right like it was leaning into wind.

*Alice — Five errors. You missed 12-Down. Yours in outrage, B.*

Alice laughed so hard the aide came in to check on her.

---

It went on for eleven weeks. Mallory was the channel. Everything passed through her: the small complaints, the reports on the pigeons, the argument about whether *Casablanca* was overrated (Bob said yes, purely to provoke), the day Alice's daughter called and didn't call again, the day Bob's oxygen was turned up.

And somewhere in the fourth or fifth week — Mallory could not have named the day — she started reading them.

It was not, at first, malice. It was three in the morning on a fourteen-hour shift, and the corridor smelled like bleach and the letter was right there in her pocket. She told herself she was checking that they were all right. That was true. It just wasn't the whole truth. The whole truth was that Mallory was lonely in a way she had no vocabulary for, and these two old people had built something warm and lit, and she stood outside it holding the door.

So she read. And then she began to edit.

Small things. Bob wrote, *My chest was bad last night but it's nothing.* Mallory copied it out fresh, in her own careful print, and left out the first clause, because why should Alice lie awake? Alice wrote, *I'm frightened, Bob,* and Mallory wrote instead, *It's been a long week, but the pigeons are thriving.* She told herself she was protecting them. She was a nurse. Protecting was the job.

But it kept going. She began adding. A joke here, because Bob's joke had been weak and Alice deserved better. A question there, because Alice hadn't asked one and Bob liked being asked. She built a bridge between them out of her own hands and did not tell either of them she was standing on it.

By June, roughly a third of what passed between Cedar and Birch had been written by a twenty-four-year-old in the third-floor supply closet.

---

In July they opened the wings.

Mallory found out on a Thursday and felt her stomach go through the floor. She had one day. She spent it in a kind of controlled panic, trying to reconstruct what she had told each of them, what each of them believed the other had said — and realized, with a clarity that made her sit down on an overturned bucket, that it was not reconstructible. She had told Alice that Bob's granddaughter was named Rose. She had no idea where she'd gotten that. She had told Bob that Alice had been a schoolteacher. Alice had been a claims adjuster.

She thought about calling in sick.

Instead she went to Alice's room, and sat on the edge of the bed, and said, "I have to tell you something, and then I'll probably lose my job."

She told her all of it. Alice listened with her hands folded, the way she must have listened to a thousand people explaining a thousand accidents.

When Mallory finished, Alice said, "How long have you known you were doing it?"

"About a month."

"And you kept doing it."

"Yes."

Alice nodded slowly. "Well," she said. "That's the honest answer, at least."

---

They met in the courtyard the next morning, Alice and Bob, under the awning, six feet apart because some habits take longer to die than others. Bob had shaved. Alice had done something to her hair.

"You never taught school," he said.

"No."

"You're not sorry about it."

"Not remotely."

He nodded. Then he said, "My granddaughter's name is Diane."

"I know," said Alice. "I know now."

They sat with it. Somewhere behind the glass, Mallory was pretending to restock a cart and failing.

"The thing is," Bob said at last, "I read them fifty times each. And I could always tell. Not consciously. But there were letters where you were *there*, and letters where something was standing where you should have been." He looked at his hands. "I liked the ones with you in them better. Even the bad news. *Especially* the bad news."

"She was trying to spare us."

"I know what she was trying to do." He said it without heat. "I've been spared before. It's not as good as people think."

---

They did not report her. Alice said the girl had worked eleven weeks of doubles and had carried, by her own count, four hundred pieces of paper up and down two flights of stairs for people who could not walk them, and that whatever else she'd done, that part was real.

But there was a condition, and Bob delivered it, in the hallway, in his wind-leaning voice.

"Anything you want to say to us," he said, "you say to us. Signed. In your own name."

Mallory started to answer and found she couldn't.

"You wanted to be in it," Alice said, not unkindly. "So be in it. But be in it as yourself."

So there were three of them after that, in the courtyard, most mornings, arguing about the crossword. And it turned out Mallory was terrible at crosswords, genuinely, embarrassingly bad, which was the first thing about her that either of them had learned firsthand — and both of them, in their separate ways, found it enormously reassuring.

# The Man in the Middle

Alice Nwosu had been leaving notes in the hollow of the sycamore since she was nine years old.

Back then the notes had been about earthworms and a boy in her class who chewed erasers. Now she was thirty-four, and the notes were about her mother's oncologist, and the mortgage, and the way the house creaked at 3 a.m. like it was trying to tell her something.

Bob Feldstein lived on the other side of the sycamore, in the yellow house with the sagging porch. He'd been eleven when the notes started. He was the one who'd suggested the hollow in the first place, having read about dead drops in a paperback thriller his father left behind. They had invented a cipher that summer — a wheel of two cardboard discs, shift the inner ring three letters, and *hello* became *khoor*. They had believed, with the total conviction of children, that this made them uncrackable.

They were adults now. Bob repaired pianos. Alice taught eighth-grade earth science. Neither of them had ever said the thing out loud, and so the notes continued, because notes were easier.

*The scan was clean,* Alice wrote in November. *I cried in the parking garage for twenty minutes. I don't know if it was relief.*

*It was relief,* Bob wrote back. *Relief comes out sideways. Come over. I'll make the soup with too much dill that you pretend to like.*

She came over. She ate the soup. She did not pretend; she had always actually liked the dill. They sat on the sagging porch and watched the sycamore go bare, and neither of them said the thing, and at ten-thirty she walked the eighty feet home.

---

Mallory Quinn moved into the rental between them in January.

She was pleasant in the way that a well-designed lobby is pleasant. She brought over a bundt cake. She learned both their names inside a week and asked good questions and remembered the answers. Bob thought she was lonely. Alice thought she was something else, but couldn't have said what, and felt petty for thinking it.

Mallory noticed the tree in her third week. Not the tree — the *habit*. Alice pausing on her walk to work, hand dipping into the trunk like a woman checking a mailbox she was embarrassed to own. Bob, at dusk, doing the same.

It took Mallory four days to find the hollow. It took her one evening with a legal pad to break a Caesar cipher with a shift of three.

She should have stopped there. She would say later, to herself, in the small hours, that she had meant to stop there.

But the notes were *good*. They were the best thing Mallory had read in years — two people saying true things carefully, over decades, in a code a child could break. Her own life had been a series of clean exits: three cities, two marriages, a career in claims adjustment that had taught her the precise dollar value of everything a person could lose. Nobody had ever left her a note in a tree.

So she started editing.

Small things at first. Alice wrote: *I think I want to sell the house. Is that insane?* Mallory copied it out in Alice's slanted capitals, shifted three, and changed *Is that insane?* to *I think I need to be somewhere new. Somewhere without all this.*

Bob read it three times on his porch. Then he wrote back: *You should do what makes you happy.* Which Mallory intercepted, and which became: *You should do what makes you happy. I've been thinking about that too, actually.*

It was so easy. That was the terrible part. She had assumed there would be some friction, some moment where the machine caught. But the cipher was a cardboard wheel, and the hollow was a hole in a tree, and love, it turned out, had no authentication whatsoever.

By March, Alice believed Bob was pulling away. By April, Bob believed Alice had someone else, someone in the city, someone she'd mentioned once — a mention Mallory had invented at 11 p.m. on a Tuesday with a glass of wine at her elbow.

The notes got shorter. Then formal. Then they stopped.

Mallory sat in the rental with a shoebox of the originals — she had kept every one, she couldn't have said why — and understood that she had built a beautiful silence and had nowhere to put it.

---

In May, Bob's washing machine flooded, and he knocked on Alice's door to borrow a wet-vac, and neither of them had spoken in six weeks, and it was so awkward that Alice laughed.

"This is stupid," she said, in her doorway, in her mother's old cardigan.

"Which part."

"You tell me. You're the one who's been —" She stopped. Started over. "Bob. Just say it out loud. Whatever it is. Say it with your *mouth*."

He stood there in the rain with a bucket. And because he was tired, and because the alternative was another six weeks, he said the thing.

It took about four seconds. Twenty-five years, four seconds.

Alice stared at him. "Then what was all that? The note about needing to be somewhere new?"

"You wrote that."

"I *never* wrote that."

They stood there. Then, very slowly, both of them turned and looked at the rental house between them, where a light was on, and a shadow moved away from the window.

---

Mallory left on a Saturday. She didn't say goodbye, but she left the shoebox on Alice's step with a rubber band around it and a single sheet on top, uncoded, in her own handwriting.

It said: *I'm sorry. It's not an excuse but I want you to know I never lost one. I read them all twice. You should keep writing them, but not in the tree.*

Alice read it on the step. Bob read it over her shoulder.

They kept the shoebox. They filled in the hollow with concrete, which felt dramatic but also correct. And they got married the following autumn under the sycamore, which Bob's brother pointed out was a little on the nose.

Sometimes, still, Alice writes Bob a note. She uses the cardboard wheel. Shift of three.

But now she hands it to him directly, and watches his face while he reads.

**The Third Party**

Alice ran the post office in Kestrel Falls, which meant she knew everyone's business and had the discipline never to mention it. She knew that Mrs. Doohan ordered her romance novels in plain brown wrappers. She knew that the Petersen boy was writing to a girl in Manitoba and that the letters had stopped coming back in March. She sorted all of it, stamped all of it, and said nothing, because that was the job.

Bob ran the hardware store across the square. For eleven years he had come in every Tuesday to mail a package to his mother in Duluth, and for eleven years he had stood at the counter afterward, turning his cap in his hands, saying something about the weather. Alice had a theory that Bob's mother received a great many unnecessary packages.

Mallory was new.

She'd taken the apartment above the laundromat in September and had, within a month, made herself indispensable in the way certain people can. She fixed the church's boiler. She organized a食 drive. She had a laugh you could hear across the square, and she used Alice's first name from the second day, which nobody in Kestrel Falls did before the second year.

She also began sending letters.

Not many — one a week, always to a post office box in the city, always in the same cream envelope, always without a return address. Alice noticed because noticing was her nature, and she said nothing because saying nothing was her discipline.

Then, in November, a letter came *back*.

It was addressed to Mallory, from that same box, and Alice held it a moment longer than she needed to. The handwriting on it was familiar. She'd seen it eleven years of Tuesdays, on eleven years of packages to Duluth.

It was Bob's.

---

Here is what Alice did with that information: nothing.

She put the letter in Mallory's box. She wished Mrs. Doohan a good morning. She stamped and sorted and closed at five. And when Bob came in that Tuesday, cap in hand, and said that it looked like snow, Alice agreed that it did look like snow.

But she thought about it. She thought about it a great deal.

The obvious story was ugly and she resisted it, because she liked Bob, and because she had come, despite herself, to like Mallory too. Still, the ugly story kept assembling itself in her head at night like a jigsaw doing itself: the new woman, the lonely man, the letters routed through a box in the city so that no one in Kestrel Falls would see the envelopes pass directly between them.

In December, Mallory came in with a cream envelope and said, "You've been quiet with me lately."

"I'm quiet with everyone."

"You're quiet *at* everyone. With me you've gone silent." Mallory set the envelope on the counter and didn't let go of it. "You've seen the letters."

"I see all the letters. It's the job."

"Ask me, then."

Alice looked at her a long moment. Outside, the snow that had been looking like snow for a month was finally getting on with it.

"It's not my business," Alice said.

"It is, though." Mallory pushed the envelope across. "Open it."

"I can't open mail."

"You can open mail you're given." Mallory's face did something complicated. "Please."

So Alice opened it.

Inside was not a letter. It was a photocopy of a court document, and a sheet of Bob's careful block capitals, and a photograph of a woman about sixty with Bob's exact chin.

"His sister," Mallory said. "Deborah. She's been in the state hospital nine years and the county's been trying to move her to a facility three hundred miles away because it's cheaper. Bob can't fight it alone — he doesn't have the money and he doesn't have the words. I used to be a paralegal. Before." She tapped the envelope. "The box in the city belongs to a lawyer who's doing this for free and doesn't want her firm to know. Bob writes to her. She writes back through me because Bob was terrified—" Mallory stopped. "He was terrified you'd see. He didn't want the whole town knowing about Deborah. He's ashamed, which is stupid, but there it is."

Alice looked at the photograph. The woman was laughing at something outside the frame.

"Eleven years of packages to Duluth," Alice said slowly.

"There's no mother in Duluth. There's a friend who forwards them to the hospital, because Bob didn't want the address on anything anybody here might handle." Mallory shook her head. "Eleven years, Alice. He built an entire architecture of secrets so a woman who never says a word about anybody's business wouldn't find out about his sister."

Alice was quiet.

"I told him he was being ridiculous," Mallory said. "He said you'd think less of him."

"I've never thought less of anyone in this room in my life," Alice said, and was surprised to find her voice unsteady.

---

The hearing was in February. Alice closed the post office for the first time in nine years and hung a sign that said FAMILY MATTER, which was true enough, and the three of them drove down together in Mallory's rattling truck with the heater that only worked on the passenger side.

They won. Not entirely — they never win entirely — but Deborah stayed within visiting distance, and in April Bob brought her to the square on a Saturday and introduced her to everyone, and the town, being a town, absorbed her in about ten minutes.

That Tuesday, Bob came in with a package addressed to a hospital forty miles away, plainly, no fiction about it. He stood at the counter turning his cap in his hands.

"Looks like rain," he said.

"It does," said Alice, and stamped it, and smiled.

# The Interceptor

Alice worked the night shift at the bottling plant and left notes for Bob under the third paving stone by the mailboxes, because neither of them owned a phone that could be trusted, and because it was more romantic that way.

That was her word for it. Bob's word was *inefficient*. But he still checked the stone every morning at six-fifteen, crouching in the blue dark with his coffee balanced on his knee, prying up the corner with a butter knife he kept in his coat pocket for exactly this purpose.

*The supervisor found the shortcut through the loading dock,* she wrote. *Now we all have to walk around. Twelve extra steps each way, eight times a shift. I calculated it. I thought of you when I calculated it.*

*You thought of me because of arithmetic,* Bob wrote back. *I'll take it.*

They had been doing this for four months. They lived in the same building. Apartment 3C and apartment 5A, two floors and one narrow stairwell apart, and they could have simply knocked. Alice had explained her reasoning once and Bob had pretended to understand it: that a knock was a demand, and a note was a gift; that anything left under a stone had to be *wanted* to be found.

Mallory found the first one in October.

She lived in 1B, ground floor, window facing the mailboxes, and she had not been sleeping well since her husband moved to Tucson with a woman who sold essential oils. At three in the morning she watched a woman in a bottling-plant uniform kneel by the walkway and slide a folded paper under a stone, and then look around like a thief, and then smile like a girl.

Mallory waited until the hallway light clicked off. Then she went outside in her slippers and took it.

*I dreamed the machines were singing,* the note said. *Not words. Just the sound they make, but arranged. I woke up and I wanted to tell someone and you were the someone.*

Mallory sat on her kitchen floor with her back against the dishwasher and read it eleven times.

She meant to put it back. Instead she copied it out longhand onto a sheet of her own paper, folded it the same way — thirds, then half — and returned the copy to the stone. She kept the original in the drawer with the takeout menus.

She told herself this was not stealing. Nothing had been lost. The message had arrived.

It became a practice. Every few days: retrieve, transcribe, replace. She grew fast at it. She learned Alice's handwriting the way you learn a song, all those tall looping *l*'s, the way she crossed her *t*'s at a hopeful upward angle. She learned Bob's too — cramped, engineer's print, but the jokes hidden in it like coins in a couch.

*My mother asked if I was seeing anyone,* Bob wrote. *I said I was corresponding with someone. She asked if that was a euphemism. I said not yet.*

Mallory laughed out loud at that one, alone, at four in the morning, and then put her hand over her mouth in the empty apartment.

In December, Alice's father got sick.

*I don't know how to write this so I'm just going to write it,* the note said. *He doesn't recognize me. He recognizes the nurse. He calls her by my name. I sat there for two hours and I was the stranger and she was the daughter and I couldn't correct him because it made him happy.*

Mallory copied it out and her hand shook and the letters came out wrong, too much like her own, and she had to start over twice.

Bob's reply came the next morning: *I'm going to break the rule. Come upstairs. Bring nothing. Knock.*

Mallory read it four times. Then she folded it into thirds, then half, and put it back under the stone, and she did not copy it, because she understood that copying it would mean keeping something that had just become too heavy to hold.

She stopped after that.

---

In February the building's pipes froze and everyone stood out in the parking lot at eleven at night while a man from the city did something with a wrench. Alice was there in a parka with her hood up. Bob was there holding two coffees. Mallory recognized them instantly and completely, the way you recognize a face from a photograph you have looked at too long.

"You're 1B," Alice said. "I've seen you at the mailboxes."

"Mallory."

"Alice. This is Bob."

Bob handed her one of the coffees. "Take it. I brought two out of habit and she only drinks tea now."

Mallory took it. The cup was very hot through her gloves.

"You always have your light on," Alice said. "At night. I see it when I come home. It's — I don't know. It's nice. Like someone's awake."

Mallory looked at her. She thought of the drawer with the takeout menus, forty-one folded pages in a rubber band, the singing machines, the twelve extra steps, the nurse with the borrowed name.

"Someone usually is," she said.

Later she went inside and got the drawer and sat with it a long while. She did not burn them; that felt operatic. In the end she put them in an envelope with no name on it and slid it under the third paving stone, where it would be found by whoever wanted it enough to look.

Then she went upstairs, two floors, one narrow stairwell, and stood outside 5A with her hand raised.

She had never learned how to leave a note. But she knew how to knock.

**The Woman in the Middle**

Mallory Chen had been sorting mail at the Ridgeline Post Office for eleven years, and in that time she had developed a theory: you could tell everything about a person from their envelopes.

Bill collectors used windowed envelopes, thin as onion skin. Grandmothers used the kind with flowers printed inside so no one could see the check. And people in love — people genuinely, foolishly in love — used whatever they could find, because they had already written the letter and could not bear to wait until Tuesday to buy proper stationery.

Which is how she came to know about Alice and Bob.

The first one came in October, addressed in a slanted hand to *Robert Ostrowski, 14 Halloway Lane*, from an *A. Marchetti* in Portland. The envelope was a repurposed utility bill, taped shut, the return address scrawled over the printed one. Mallory turned it over twice before she put it in Bob's slot.

She knew Bob. Everyone knew Bob. He ran the hardware store on Main and had a laugh you could hear from the pharmacy across the street, and he had spent three years being very, very quiet after his wife died. He came in Thursdays for his packages, always apologized for the trouble, always brought her a coffee she hadn't asked for.

The second letter came nine days later. The third came four days after that. By November they were arriving twice a week, and Mallory — who was not proud of this, who told herself it was simply an occupational hazard — had begun to look forward to them.

She never opened one. She wants that on the record. She never steamed a seal or slit a corner. But she noticed things. She noticed when Alice switched from taped envelopes to a proper box of cream-colored ones, which meant she had started taking this seriously. She noticed when Bob started coming in on Tuesdays *and* Thursdays. She noticed the November when a letter came back marked **RETURN TO SENDER — REFUSED**, in Bob's blocky hardware-store printing, and how it sat in her hands like something with a pulse.

She thought about it for two days. Then she did the thing she still cannot fully justify.

She wrote *DELIVERED IN ERROR* on the envelope, scratched out Bob's refusal, and sent it back to him.

---

He came in that Thursday with two coffees, as always, and set one on her counter, and did not say anything for a long moment.

"You did this," he said.

"Did what."

"Mallory."

She squared a stack of forms that did not need squaring. "There's a lot of mail that moves through here. Sometimes it goes in circles."

Bob looked at the ceiling. He was a big man and he had a way of getting smaller when something hurt. "Her name's Alice. We met at my sister's thing in Portland. In September." He turned the coffee cup a quarter turn on the counter. "She's got a whole life there. Job, house, a kid in college. And I've got — this." He gestured vaguely at the town, the street, the hardware store, the whole small geometry of it.

"So she should stop writing."

"She should stop *hoping*." He said it too loudly, then winced. "I'm sixty-one years old. I already had my one good thing. It seems greedy to ask for another."

Mallory considered this. Outside, someone's truck failed to start, tried again, succeeded.

"Do you know what happens to mail nobody claims?" she said.

"No."

"It goes to a facility in Atlanta. They open it. They try to find someone who wants it. And if nobody does, they auction off whatever's inside and pulp the rest." She slid his packages across the counter. "Eleven years I've been doing this, Bob. The saddest thing I ever handle isn't the bad news. It's the letters that made it all the way here and then stopped one door short."

---

The refused letter, as it turned out, had contained a train schedule.

Alice arrived on the 3:40 the Saturday before Thanksgiving. Mallory only knows this because she was walking back from the diner and saw them on the platform — a small woman in an enormous coat, and Bob standing about four feet too far away, the way people do when they're afraid of getting it wrong. Then not four feet. Then not any feet at all.

Mallory kept walking. It seemed like the decent thing.

---

The letters stopped in March, which frightened her for about a week, until she understood: they'd stopped because Alice's mail now came addressed to *14 Halloway Lane* directly, forwarded from Portland, boxes and boxes of it, a whole life relocating one parcel at a time.

Bob still comes in Thursdays. He brings two coffees. Sometimes Alice comes with him and brings a third for herself, and she has a laugh that pairs disgracefully well with his, and the two of them clog up the lobby talking to whoever's in line.

Last month Alice hung back while Bob wrestled a mailer of cabinet hinges out to the truck.

"He told me," she said.

Mallory kept her eyes on the scale. "Told you what."

"That a letter came back to him that he'd already sent away." Alice leaned on the counter. "He said the post office made a mistake."

"The post office makes lots of mistakes."

"Mm." Alice smiled — a slow, knowing, entirely unfooled smile. "Well. I'm grateful for the incompetence."

Mallory finally looked up. "You understand I could lose my job."

"For delivering mail?"

"For interfering."

Alice picked up her coffee and turned toward the door, where Bob was waving at her through the glass like an idiot, like a man with an unreasonable amount of luck.

"Mallory," she said, "you didn't interfere. You just refused to be the place where it stopped."

And she went out into the cold, and the bell above the door rang, and Mallory Chen went back to sorting the mail — the bills, the flowered envelopes, the ordinary miracles, all of it passing through her hands on the way to somewhere else.

**The Dumbwaiter**

The building on Pell Street was old enough to have a dumbwaiter and stubborn enough to keep it. It ran between the fourth floor and the sixth, a little wooden box on frayed ropes, and it had not carried soup in sixty years.

Alice lived in 4B. Bob lived in 6B. They had never met.

It began with a misdelivered package — a book of crossword puzzles that belonged to Bob and arrived at Alice's door. Alice, who did not like stairs and liked strangers even less, put the book in the dumbwaiter with a note that said, *I think this is yours. Sorry, 47-Across was too tempting. — A, 4B*

Bob wrote back: *You got it wrong. It's ANEMONE, not ANATHEMA. Though I understand the confusion. — B, 6B*

And so it went.

What neither of them knew was that the dumbwaiter's rope ran through a service closet on the fifth floor, and that the service closet belonged to Mallory, who had been the superintendent of the building on Pell Street for nineteen years.

Mallory was not a bad person. Mallory would like that on the record. But Mallory was sixty-three, widowed, and had recently discovered that the hours between eight and eleven at night were the longest hours ever invented. So when the little box came creaking down past the fifth floor with a folded paper in it, Mallory stopped the rope, and read.

The first few, Mallory only read.

*I work at the county records office,* Alice wrote in October. *People come in looking for their grandmothers. I find them. It is not exciting but it is not nothing.*

*I fix watches,* Bob wrote. *Or I did. My hands shake now. Mostly I take them apart and look at them and put them back the way they were.*

Mallory read that one three times, then sent it up.

The trouble started in November.

Bob wrote: *There's a bakery on Ninth that does a cardamom bun on Saturdays. I go at seven when they come out of the oven. If you ever wanted to see what I look like, that's where I'd be.*

Mallory held the paper for a long moment under the bare closet bulb. Then Mallory thought about Alice in 4B, who had not left the apartment except for work in — Mallory checked the mental ledger every super keeps — four years. Since the accident with her husband's car. Mallory thought about how an invitation like that, arriving too early, could end a thing rather than begin it.

Mallory took a pen from the toolbox and copied the note out, in a shaky hand not so different from Bob's, and left out the last two sentences.

Alice's reply came down light and easy. Nothing had broken.

After that it was harder to stop.

When Bob wrote *I suppose you're married,* Mallory changed it to *I suppose you have people.* When Alice wrote *I'm sorry, I've been in a mood, ignore me,* Mallory sent up instead: *Tell me about the watches again.* When Bob mentioned his son in Tacoma who never called, Mallory let that one through whole, and then sat on the closet floor for an hour with the dust and the rope smell.

By January the notes were coming twice a day and Mallory was editing both directions, softening, tuning, the way you'd adjust a hairspring — a quarter turn, no more. Mallory told himself it was maintenance. That is, after all, what a superintendent does. He keeps the building from falling down on the people inside it.

In February the rope broke.

It broke at four in the afternoon with a sound like a cough, and the box fell two floors and split its corner, and there was nothing in it but a note, and Mallory picked it up off the shaft floor because Mallory was the one who came when things broke.

It was from Bob, and it said: *I'm going into the hospital Thursday. It isn't serious but they say it isn't nothing. I have never asked you for anything. I'm asking now. Come.*

Mallory stood in the shaft with the note.

Here is the thing Mallory understood, standing there: that for four months he had been the only person in the building who knew both of them, and he had used that to keep them at a distance he found comfortable, and he had called it kindness. That a man can steal something without ever taking it anywhere. That he had been lonely and had built himself a room out of other people's sentences and lived in it.

He climbed the stairs to 4B. It took him a while; his knees were nineteen years older than they'd been.

Alice opened the door with the chain on.

"The dumbwaiter's broken," Mallory said. "I can't fix it. I'm sorry." He held the note through the gap. "This came before it went."

She read it. Her face did something complicated.

"He said the hospital," she said. "He never — he doesn't say things like this."

"He does," Mallory said. "He has been. I'm the one who didn't say them."

She looked up at him then, and Mallory made himself stand in it.

"Get your coat," he said. "It's Thursday. I've got the van."

She did not forgive him. Not that year, and maybe not entirely, ever. But she got her coat.

The three of them sat in a beige room on the fourth floor of St. Vincent's, and Bob said, "You're shorter than your handwriting," and Alice laughed with her hand over her mouth, and Mallory sat by the door, where a man sits when he has finally decided to be only a door.
